title: How Hurricanes Look From Space Station
description: Astronauts aboard the International Space Station observe massive hurricane systems moving across Earth's oceans. Weather satellites continuously monitor these storms from tens of thousands of kilometres away.

shots.narration: From orbit, a hurricane reveals its quiet center and the intense storm system surrounding it.
The central eye is typically 30 to 65 km wide and almost calm.
The strongest winds blow in the eyewall directly surrounding this quiet center.
In a category 5 storm, eyewall winds exceed 250 km/h.
A mature hurricane releases heat at a rate about 200 times the world's electricity generation.
These storms spin anticlockwise north of the equator and clockwise south of it.
A large hurricane can measure more than 1,000 km across.
The space station crosses one of these massive systems in about two minutes.
Farther out, GOES weather satellites watch from 35,800 km up, imaging a storm every thirty seconds.
